pronunciation.approximation: FRAY-ya — the first syllable is the diphthong ey, close to English 'ay' in 'say' with rounded lips; stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ja sounds like English 'ya'.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Freyja is the common noun freyja, 'lady', used as a proper name — the feminine counterpart of her brother's name Freyr, 'lord'. Both descend from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ, and the cognate line runs through Old High German frouwa to the modern German Frau. Freyja is Tier 2 by rule: the normalized Old Norse spelling is plain Latin letters, so the ASCII form loses nothing — there is no diacritic, no thorn, no eth to restore. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by capitalization.

domains.title: The Lady of the Vanir
domains.subtitle: Brísingamen, Seiðr, and the Choice of the Slain
domains.lead: Freyja is the preeminent goddess of the Norse pantheon: a Vanir among the Æsir, mistress of seiðr magic, owner of the necklace Brísingamen, rider of a chariot drawn by cats, and chooser of half the slain — for she keeps a hall, Sessrúmnir in the field Fólkvangr, and divides the battle-dead with Óðinn himself.

cards.name: Brísingamen
cards.desc: The necklace of the Brísings, Freyja's great treasure — the jewel Loki steals and Heimdallr wins back, fighting for it in seal-shape.

cards.name: The Cat-Drawn Chariot
cards.desc: Freyja drives a wagon pulled by two cats — the only chariot-team of its kind in the Eddas, and the image her cult made famous.

cards.name: The Falcon Cloak
cards.desc: Her valshamr, the falcon-feather coat that lets the wearer fly between worlds — borrowed twice by Loki, and coveted by the giant Þjazi.

cards.name: Fólkvangr
cards.desc: 'The field of the host', Freyja's domain among the slain: her hall there is Sessrúmnir, 'seat-roomy', and half the battle-dead are hers.

symbols.name: Brísingamen
symbols.meaning: The necklace that is worth any price — beauty, desire, and the things a goddess will not be commanded to trade

symbols.name: The cats
symbols.meaning: Her chariot-team: the household animal elevated to divine harness, love and independence in one pair

symbols.name: The falcon-feather cloak
symbols.meaning: The garment of flight — the power to cross worlds that others must borrow from her

symbols.name: Tears of red gold
symbols.meaning: The weeping for the absent Óðr — the myth the skalds built into the kenning 'Freyja's tears' for gold

symbols.name: Hildisvíni
symbols.meaning: 'Battle-swine', the boar she rides in Hyndluljóðr — the Vanir animal of fertility under a warrior's name

mythology.lead: Freyja is everywhere in the Norse corpus: the Poetic Edda, Snorri's prose, and the opening chapters of Heimskringla all circle her — her hall among the dead, her magic, her necklace, her lost husband, and the flyting in which Loki names her last.

myths.title: Fólkvangr and the Half of the Slain
myths.text: Snorri places Freyja beside Frigg as foremost among the goddesses, and gives her what no other goddess has: a share of the battle-dead. 'Her hall is called Sessrúmnir, and it is large and fair. Whenever she rides to battle, she takes half of the slain, and half belong to Óðinn.' Her field is Fólkvangr, the folk-plain; her hall is 'seat-roomy'. The Grímnismál preserves the same division in verse — Freyja chooses the half of the slain each day, Óðinn the other — so the doctrine is older than Snorri: the Lord of the Slain does not keep them all. The Lady keeps a war-dead of her own.

myths.title: She Taught the Æsir Seiðr
myths.text: Heimskringla's euhemerized history makes Freyja the magic's transmitter: 'Freyja was a blótgyðja, a sacrificial priestess, and she was the first to teach the Æsir seiðr, which had been customary among the Vanir.' Seiðr — the far-reaching, fate-working magic that let its practitioner know the future and shape events — was Vanir craft, and it crossed into the Æsir's world through her; Ynglinga saga adds that Óðinn himself learned it and wielded it beyond anyone. Modern scholarship on seiðr, above all Neil Price's work, treats this notice as the tradition's own memory of a real ritual complex — staffs, seeresses, and performances attested in sagas and graves alike.

myths.title: The Hammer-Ransom
myths.text: When the giant Þrymr steals Mjölnir and names his price — Freyja as his bride — the gods bring her the offer. Her refusal is one of the Poetic Edda's great moments: 'Freyja was enraged, and snorted, so that the whole hall of the Æsir shook beneath her, and the great necklace of the Brísings burst: “You will know me to be most mad for a man, if I drive with you to the realm of the giants.”' No marriage happens. Instead Þórr is dressed in Freyja's bridal linen, with the necklace Brísingamen at his throat and Loki as his handmaid, and goes to Jötunheimr as the false bride — recovering the hammer under the veil. The poem's joke rests on a fixed point: Freyja cannot be given away; she can only be impersonated.

myths.title: Óttarr, Hildisvíni, and the Giantess Hyndla
myths.text: Freyja protects her devotee Óttarr, who has wagered his inheritance on his ancestry, and carries him to the giantess Hyndla to force out the genealogy he needs. She has transformed Óttarr into her boar Hildisvíni, 'battle-swine', and rides him to the giantess's cave; when Hyndla sees through the shape, Freyja answers without flinching and compels the recitation anyway, demanding the memory-ale that will let Óttarr keep the lore through his lawsuit. The poem also preserves, in its catalogue of Óðinn's gifts, the standing notice that Freyja rides to battle and takes her due of the slain — the prose doctrine of Gylfaginning in older verse.

myths.title: Óðr, the Tears of Gold, and the Many Names
myths.text: Skáldskaparmál assembles Freyja's poetic dossier. Her husband is Óðr; their daughters are Hnoss and Gersimi — 'Treasure' and 'Gem' — names so precious that what is costly is still called by them. Óðr went away on long journeys, and Freyja weeps for him, 'and her tears are red gold' — the myth behind the skaldic kenning that calls gold Freyja's tears. Snorri lists her aliases: Vanadís, 'the dís of the Vanir'; Hörn; Gefn; Sýr, 'Sow'; Mardöll — and she is called Valfreyja, 'Lady of the Slain'. The necklace appears too: gold may be called 'Brísingamen' for her, and Húsdrápa remembers that Loki and Heimdallr once fought for the jewel at Singasteinn, each in the shape of a seal.

myths.title: The Flyting
myths.text: In Loki's feast of insults, Freyja speaks against him and receives the flyting's standard charge — that she has been the lover of all in the hall, Æsir and elves alike. Njǫrðr her father answers for her: 'It is no great harm though a woman gets herself a man, a husband or a lover or both.' The exchange is the Edda's shorthand for what the whole corpus shows: Freyja's sexuality is hers, ungoverned by the marriage bargains others try to make of her — and the tradition itself, in Njǫrðr's voice, declines to call it shame.

lore.syncretism: Freyja's most consequential kinship is internal: her relationship to Frigg. Both are chief goddesses, both own a falcon cloak, both weep for an absent husband (Óðr's name is one consonant from Óðinn's), and scholarship from the nineteenth century onward has debated whether the two were originally one goddess split by the traditions that recorded them — a question the sources leave open and handbooks like Simek and Orchard still mark as unsettled. The interpretatio latina equated her with Venus, and the Germanic week keeps the trace: Friday, dies Veneris, 'the Lady's day' — though whether the day was named for Freyja or for Frigg is itself part of the same debate. Beyond Germania there is no borrowing to claim: the Vanir package — fertility, wealth, magic, and a share of the dead — is the North's own construction, and the goddess who taught seiðr to the Æsir has no exact counterpart anywhere else.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Norse goddess has a longer afterlife. Wagner fused Freyja with Iðunn into Freia, the goddess of youth whose ransom opens the Ring cycle, and the Victorian mythographies made her the Venus of the North. In the twentieth century she became central to modern Heathenry and Ásatrú, where she is honored as mistress of seiðr and patron of the half of the slain — and to the revival of seiðr practice that scholars and practitioners alike trace to her teaching in Ynglinga saga. Her name never died in Scandinavia: Freyja is a living, and increasingly popular, girls' given name in Iceland and across the North. And the week still speaks her cognate every Friday — the Lady's day, whichever goddess the chronology finally credits.
lore.extendedMeditation: Freyja holds two things the world keeps trying to separate. She is the goddess of love — desire, gold, the necklace, the weeping for Óðr — and she is a commander of the dead, choosing half the slain before Óðinn takes his half. The Edda refuses the split: the same figure who weeps tears of red gold rides to battle; the same name that means 'lady' heads a war-dead of her own. The restoration Freyja needs no diacritics to make the point — the word itself is the argument. In Old Norse, to say 'the lady' was to say her name. The title and the goddess are one word, and the one word is enough.

sources.name: Orchard, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend

lore.archaeology: Freyja's attestations are textual — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda's codices (13th-14th c.), with skaldic verse centuries older — but her world has a material record. The theophoric place-names of Sweden and Norway are dense with the Frö-/Frøy- element, though most are assigned to her brother Freyr; a smaller set (Norway's Frøya island among them) is argued either way. The seiðr she taught the Æsir is the best-attested ritual complex in the graves: the 'völva burials' of Viking-Age Scandinavia, with their iron staffs, high-status grave goods, and in some cases mind-altering seeds, are the material context Neil Price's The Viking Way reads as the practice's archaeology. Small silver pendants of standing female figures, once loosely called valkyries, have been reinterpreted in the same frame — the tradition's seeress and its Lady overlap in the metal as they do in the verse.
lore.originalScriptNote: Old Norse literature was transmitted in medieval Icelandic manuscripts written in the Latin alphabet; the earlier epigraphic medium was the Younger Futhark. The theonym Freyja is known from the manuscript tradition; a hypothetical runic rendering would approximate ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛁᛅ (f-r-au-i-a). Unusually among the restorations, the normalized Old Norse form needs nothing ASCII lacks: Freyja is already the attested spelling, letter for letter — a Tier-2 name whose restoration is complete in plain Latin. The plain-ASCII domain freyja.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection by a third party; the project watches it for release and keeps this temple canonical under the /sites/freyja/ path in the meantime.
